title: The Middle Assyrian Kingdom
subtitle: 1400–1050 BC · Assur throws off Mitanni, the Empire and Murder of Tukulti-Ninurta, the Revival of Tiglath-Pileser I, and the Aramaean Flood

categories.label: Power
categories.subtitle: Ashur-uballit's founding of the Assyrian state, the conquest of Mitanni, the brief empire and murder of Tukulti-Ninurta, the whirlwind revival under Tiglath-Pileser I, and the reduction of Assyria to its core by the Aramaeans

entries.label: Ashur-uballit I founds the Assyrian state
entries.hint: As the kingdom of Mitanni was ground between the Hittites and Assyria, Ashur-uballit threw off its overlordship, took the title 'king of Assyria' rather than the old 'steward of the god Assur', wrote to Egypt as a fellow 'Great King', and married his granddaughter into the Kassite royal house — later marching into Babylon to avenge her son. He is the man who turned the merchant city-state of Assur into a kingdom.
entries.note: A. K. Grayson, 'Assyrian Rulers of the Third and Second Millennia BC' (RIMA 1, 1987); the Amarna letters EA 15–16 (Moran 1992).

entries.label: Adad-nirari I, the first conqueror
entries.hint: Adad-nirari I fought two wars against the rump Mitanni state of Hanigalbat, annexed it, and pushed Assyria's border to the Euphrates. He took the swaggering titles 'king of the totality' and 'king of all peoples', and his inscriptions swell from terse dedications into the boastful campaign narrative that becomes the Assyrian house style. He also beat the Kassites in a border battle at Sugagu.
entries.note: RIMA 1 (Grayson 1987); the Adad-nirari–Hanigalbat wars in the royal annals and the Hittite correspondence.

entries.label: Shalmaneser I crushes and colonises Mitanni
entries.hint: Shalmaneser I put down a Hittite-backed revolt of Hanigalbat, and — by his own count — blinded and deported fourteen thousand four hundred captives and scattered Assyrian forts and settlers across the whole dry-farming plain of the Jazira, turning the former Hurrian kingdom into an Assyrian province. He also campaigned in the Nairi highlands to the north and founded the city of Kalhu.
entries.note: RIMA 1 (Grayson 1987); the Jazira settlement in Stefan Jakob, 'Mittelassyrische Verwaltung und Sozialstruktur' (2003).

entries.label: Tukulti-Ninurta I — the peak
entries.hint: Tukulti-Ninurta I beat the Hittites, conquered Babylon and carried off both its king and its god, and campaigned deep into the Zagros and the Nairi lands. Then he built a huge new capital across the Tigris from Assur — Kar-Tukulti-Ninurta, 'Quay of Tukulti-Ninurta' — with a rival temple of Ashur 'in the new city', a move that set the old priesthood and nobility against him.
entries.note: RIMA 1 (Grayson 1987); the new capital in the excavation reports of Walter Bachmann and later German work.

entries.label: The murder of Tukulti-Ninurta
entries.hint: Besieged in his own new city by a faction of nobles, Tukulti-Ninurta was deposed and killed — Chronicle P names his son Ashur-nadin-apli as the leader. The new capital was abandoned almost at once; Assyria lost Babylon and its grip on the west; and the throne passed through a run of short reigns. The Assyrian empire's first bid ended in a palace coup.
entries.note: 'Chronicle P'; the fall in Peter Machinist, 'The Epic of Tukulti-Ninurta I' (1978), and Grayson, RIMA 1.

entries.label: The dark century
entries.hint: For most of a century Assyria was ruled by kings whose reigns are little more than names — Ashur-dan I the longest of them — under Babylonian, Elamite and steadily rising Aramaean pressure, with the western conquests lost. The records thin out. Assyria was a middling regional power holding its heartland and not much more.
entries.note: RIMA 1 (Grayson 1987); the period's obscurity noted in Marc Van De Mieroop, 'A History of the Ancient Near East' (2016).

entries.label: Ashur-resha-ishi I begins the recovery
entries.hint: Ashur-resha-ishi I beat off Aramaean raiders and repulsed a Babylonian invasion under Nebuchadnezzar I, rebuilt the temples of Assur, and restored the confidence of the Assyrian state. His reign is the platform from which his son launched the last and greatest Middle Assyrian revival.
entries.note: A. K. Grayson, 'Assyrian Rulers of the Early First Millennium BC' (RIMA 2, 1991); the clash with Nebuchadnezzar I in the Babylonian sources.

entries.label: Tiglath-Pileser I — the whirlwind
entries.hint: His clay prism claims forty-two campaigns in five years. He shattered twenty thousand Mushki — Phrygians — in the northern mountains, reached Lake Van and the Nairi lands, marched to the Mediterranean to cut cedar and take tribute from Byblos, Sidon and Arwad, sailed on the sea and speared a sea-creature, sacked Babylon, hunted elephants on the Habur and wild bulls in Lebanon, and stocked a library at Assur. It was the high-water mark of Middle Assyrian power.
entries.note: A. K. Grayson, 'Assyrian Rulers of the Early First Millennium BC I' (RIMA 2, 1991), the Tiglath-Pileser I prisms.

entries.label: Ashur-bel-kala and the rising tide
entries.hint: Ashur-bel-kala fought the Aramaeans in nearly every year of his reign — the 'Broken Obelisk' is his monument — campaigned as far as the coast, and made a marriage alliance with the Babylonian royal house. But the tribes kept crossing the Euphrates in greater numbers, and after him the effort to hold the west failed for good.
entries.note: RIMA 2 (Grayson 1991); the 'Broken Obelisk' and the Ashur-bel-kala annals.

entries.label: The reduction to the core
entries.hint: Within a generation Assyria held only the triangle of Assur, Nineveh, Arbela and Kalhu; the Aramaeans occupied the Jazira and the Habur and cut the roads west; and a poorly-recorded dark age set in that lasted until the recovery began around 934. But the state's machinery, the eponym list, the King List and the god Ashur all came through unbroken. The Neo-Assyrian Empire would be, consciously, this kingdom rebuilt.
entries.note: J. A. Brinkman, 'Prelude to Empire' (1984); the continuity of institutions in Karen Radner, 'Ancient Assyria: A Very Short Introduction' (2015).

categories.label: Conflict
categories.subtitle: The destruction of Mitanni and the deportation of its people, Tukulti-Ninurta's wars against the Hittites and Babylon, the forty-two campaigns of Tiglath-Pileser I, and the losing struggle with the Aramaean tribes

entries.label: The fall of Mitanni and the deportation of Hanigalbat
entries.hint: Over two generations Assyria dismantled the Hurrian kingdom of Mitanni — annexing its rump, Hanigalbat, under Adad-nirari I, then crushing a Hittite-backed revolt under Shalmaneser I, who reports blinding and deporting fourteen thousand four hundred people. Assyrian forts and colonists took over the emptied plain. It is the first large-scale Assyrian conquest, and the first use of mass deportation as a tool of rule.
entries.note: RIMA 1 (Grayson 1987); Stefan Jakob, 'Mittelassyrische Verwaltung und Sozialstruktur' (2003).

entries.label: The battle of Nihriya against the Hittites
entries.hint: At Nihriya on the upper Tigris, Tukulti-Ninurta defeated the army of Tudhaliya IV, the last strong king of the Hittites, in a contest over the old Mitanni lands and the metal routes through the mountains. It is one of the very few times Assyria beat a Great Power in the field, and it hastened the decline of Hatti a generation before its final collapse.
entries.note: Itamar Singer, 'The Battle of Nihriya and the End of the Hittite Empire' (ZA 1985); RIMA 1.

entries.label: The conquest of Babylon
entries.hint: Tukulti-Ninurta broke the army of the Kassite king Kashtiliash IV, took him prisoner to Assur, sacked Babylon, pulled down its wall and carried the statue of Marduk north. For about seven years an Assyrian king ruled Babylonia. His court epic presents the whole campaign as the gods' judgement on a Kassite king who had broken his sworn oath. It is the first time Assyria held the south.
entries.note: Peter Machinist, 'The Epic of Tukulti-Ninurta I' (1978); 'Chronicle P'; the Babylonian side in the folio babylon-1595bc-1155bc.

entries.label: The forty-two campaigns of Tiglath-Pileser I
entries.loc: from the Mediterranean to Lake Van
entries.hint: Tiglath-Pileser I's annals narrate a war machine at full stretch: the destruction of the Mushki in the north, campaigns into the Nairi lands and to Lake Van, the march to the sea to take Levantine tribute and cut cedar, and the sacking of Babylon. Fought almost every year, described campaign by campaign in the first person, it set the template — aggressive, annual, self-documented warfare — for the empire that came after.

entries.label: The losing struggle with the Aramaeans
entries.hint: Tiglath-Pileser I records crossing the Euphrates twenty-eight times to chase the 'Ahlamu-Aramaeans'; Ashur-bel-kala fought them yearly. It made no lasting difference. The tribes kept coming, settled the Jazira and the Habur, founded their own small states, and cut Assyria off from the west. The Middle Assyrian kingdom was not conquered so much as slowly surrounded and starved.
entries.note: K. Lawson Younger, 'A Political History of the Arameans' (2016); the annals in RIMA 2 (Grayson 1991).

entries.label: The famine and the flight to the mountains
entries.hint: Assyrian texts of the decline record years of failed harvest so severe that people abandoned their towns for the hills and — the 'Broken Obelisk' says — ate their own children. Aramaean raiding and the loss of the Jazira grain supply compounded the crop failures. The military collapse and the subsistence collapse fed each other.
entries.note: The famine passages in the Ashur-bel-kala texts (RIMA 2, Grayson 1991); discussed in Brinkman, 'Prelude to Empire' (1984).
